title: Article Archive: Leadership The Year Nobody Saw
author: Summer Mulder
summary: Summer Mulder writes about the hidden year of professional transition — the period when she was closing down one business while actively building a portfolio of new ones, holding a fixed financial line she and her husband had drawn to mark the end of the shutdown, and doing both simultaneously without public acknowledgment. The central insight is that shutting something down is not the hard part; what follows the decision is. Obligations don't dissolve when the mind moves on; they trail into whatever comes next. The piece is a meditation on boundary-holding under emotional and relational pressure — the instinct to keep going, to absorb consequences that aren't yours, to soothe others' discomfort at the cost of your own line. What kept her on that line was not willpower but people: her husband, a therapist, and entrepreneurs who had navigated similar terrain. The essay closes with a distinction the author considers essential: empathy says 'I understand this hurts'; a boundary says 'and this is still the reality.' Both can coexist.
points: The shutdown itself is not the hard part — what follows a decision to end something is a long tail of obligations, assets, and relationships that don't care that you've mentally moved on.

Holding a financial or operational line requires outside support: people who are not inside the situation and can tell you what they see from where they stand, when emotion is working to move the line.

Empathy and boundaries can coexist — 'I understand this hurts' and 'this is still the reality' are not contradictory statements, and confusing empathy with self-sacrifice is a common leadership error.
The year that produces trust in yourself is often the year no one sees — the one where you held something difficult while building something new at the same time.
quotes: What most people don't understand about shutting something down is that the shutdown isn't the hard part. What follows you is.

Things tried to move it. Emotion tried to move it. The part of me that wanted everyone to feel okay about how it ended tried to move it. The instinct to keep going just a little longer, to do just a little more, to soothe the stomach ache by proving I had done everything possible — that tried to move it too.

The mistake people make is thinking empathy requires self-sacrifice. It doesn't. Empathy is 'I understand this hurts.' A boundary is 'and this is still the reality.' Most people won't like that those two things can coexist. The reality doesn't serve them. But it has to be said anyway because the alternative is you absorbing consequences that were never yours to carry.

What kept me on the line was not willpower. It was people. My husband. My therapist. A handful of entrepreneurs who had been through something like this not once but multiple times. They had the outside perspective I couldn't manufacture for myself.

Support isn't a luxury. It's not something you earn once you've proven you can handle things alone. It's the thing that makes handling things actually possible. All the time. But especially in the moments when you can't see clearly and someone who loves you can.
